html:
A Roman silver coin brought in by the emperor Caracalla in 215. It was valued at two denarii but held only about as much silver as one and a half. The emperor wore a crown of sun rays on it, the mark of a double coin, so it is also called a radiate.

People hoarded the older, better denarii and spent the new coins, an early case of bad money driving out good. In the third-century crisis emperors needed more and more coins to pay the army, so they cut the silver again and again. By about 270 the antoninianus was a bronze coin with a thin silver wash, and prices rose fast.

Aurelian tried to fix the coinage in 274, and Diocletian replaced it with a new system in the 290s. His Edict on Maximum Prices of 301 shows that inflation had still not been beaten.
